question: Nursing informatics brings together three main fields. Which of the following makes up this combination?

options.C: Nursing science, computer science, and information science
options.D: Software engineering, hardware design, and medicine

explanation: You've got this! Nursing informatics simply blends nursing care knowledge with computer and information science to help us manage patient data smoothly. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h1)

question: When a computer processes raw data in the hospital, what does it turn that information into?
explanation: Think of it like checking vital signs: numbers alone are just raw data, but a computer helps organize them into useful clinical information for better patient care! [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h1)

question: An ECG machine tracking continuous electrical waves of the heart is an example of which type of computer?
explanation: Don't sweat this one! Analog computers work by measuring continuous physical things like waves, rather than counting discrete numbers. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h2)

question: Modern electronic health record (EHR) systems used in clinics rely on which type of processing?
explanation: Almost all the computers and hospital software we touch every day use digital processing to handle information. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which type of computer is best for a single nurse doing bedside charting?
explanation: Microcomputers are your everyday desktops, laptops, and tablets built for one user at a time—perfect for the ward! [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why do hospitals use large mainframe computers instead of regular office computers to manage hospital-wide databases?

options.A: They are exclusively dedicated to individual genomic mapping.
options.B: They are small enough to fit inside a patient medication cart.
options.C: They process continuous analog waves without electricity.
options.D: They support massive multi-user access and heavy data loads securely.

explanation: Mainframes are the heavy lifters! They have the massive power and security needed to connect every department in the hospital at once. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is another common name for a microcomputer that you probably use every day?
explanation: Spot on! Microcomputers are commonly called personal computers (PCs) because they are designed for individual use. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h4)

question: A nurse uses a handheld tablet to check medications at the bedside. What category of computer is this tablet?
explanation: Tablets and smartphones are portable and built for single users, placing them right in the microcomputer family. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which computer system is typically used to manage a specific hospital department, like the pharmacy inventory?
explanation: Minicomputers are mid-sized systems that do a fantastic job handling specific departmental jobs like lab tracking or pharmacy stock. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is a major benefit of having a mainframe computer in a large teaching hospital?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any nursing documentation at the bedside.
options.B: It functions entirely on analog wave processing principles.
options.C: It replaces the need for electrical power backups in the facility.
options.D: It integrates data across all hospital departments into one central system.

explanation: Mainframes bring everything together, making sure patient records flow seamlessly between wards, pharmacy, and the lab without getting lost. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the main job of a supercomputer in health science?

options.B: Routine nursing documentation at the bedside
options.C: Managing hospital billing and staff payroll
options.D: Complex data analysis and scientific research

explanation: Supercomputers are giants used for heavy-duty scientific research and genetic mapping, way beyond everyday ward tasks. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why won't you typically find a supercomputer on a standard nursing ward?

options.A: They are designed for massive scientific calculations rather than routine clinical workflow.
options.B: They are too small to be seen by healthcare workers.
options.C: They cannot connect to any digital network infrastructure.
options.D: They only process analog physical signals from bedside monitors.

explanation: Supercomputers are built for massive research labs, not for tracking patient meds or recording vital signs on the ward. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the main problem with using underpowered computer hardware for busy hospital databases?

options.A: Immediate destruction of all digital patient files
options.B: Automatic conversion of digital data into analog waves
options.C: System lag that delays patient care workflows
options.D: Permanent loss of electrical power across the hospital

explanation: When computers are too slow for the job, they lag. In a busy clinic, slow software means delayed patient care! [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h7)

question: A nurse manager is buying new computers for a busy accident and emergency (A&E) unit. What should guide this choice?

options.A: The physical color and brand logo of the monitor
options.B: Whether the device can perform supercomputing research
options.C: Clinical workflow needs and processing demands
options.D: The availability of analog mercury components

explanation: Always match the tool to the task! A busy emergency unit needs computers that can handle fast-paced clinical workflows without crashing. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T6#GNS113_U1_T6_h7)
